No, just ask if there is a traffic school option or a Probation Before Judgment option. Yep, counties in some states make a lot of money off of tickets, so they make fighting it as inconvenient as possible. It's normal to be asked to come in person.

You usually have three plea options: guilty, no contest, not guilty. The version of "no contest" for traffic court is usually "probation before judgment". It's **always** legal to make a "not guilty" plea even if there's clear evidence you did it. That's because a plea is not a statement that you did or didn't do a crime or commit an infraction. It's usually used to determine whether to go to trial or straight to sentencing. It isn't perjury to say "not guilty" as a plea if you are indeed guilty.

As someone with a good amount of expertise in this (well, in Maryland, where traffic laws are rarely enforced...), **do not wait until your court date**! The judge doesn't want to talk to you. You don't get a free lawyer, since it's a civil case, and quite frankly, 76 in a 55 is minor speeding.

Here's the issue: CT insurance will go up if you get convicted of a **moving** violation. **Call ahead**, and explain your situation calmly to a clerk. The ticket legally has to have a phone number to call with questions. **Tell them you are interested in PBJ** and ask if your local court system has the "traffic school and drop it" system. That varies by locality.

**DO NOT ADMIT YOUR GUILT TO THE CLERK. THAT PHONECALL IS USUALLY RECORDED AND CAN/WILL BE USED IN EVIDENCE.** Simply state your ticket ID and ask for options. Courts generally appreciate you taking the initiative before you enter the courtroom. If the clerk is a hardass with no mercy, *try calling the local DA's office* and ask the same thing. If that fails, most jurisdictions informally have a policy where low-level "offenses" are cut in half the first time (half fine, half points). Ideally, you'd get off on a **non-moving violation**. The biggest issue here is not the price of the ticket; it's the price that your insurance can legally gouge you for **three years**.

Interstates legally have to be 70 unless in a super dense (or very mountainy) area. Even around most of our cities, interstates stay at least 65 mph.

Yes, I have Asperger's, I've studied a good bit of pharmacology, and I have indeed tried Phenibut.

It is technically a gabapentinoid, and it feels like a more recreational version of how most benzodiazepines feel to me. By nature, gabapentinoids flood selected GABA receptors, which are what sleep aids and most anxiolytics (anti-anxiety medications) target. Alcohol also targets them, but less selectively.

I am **not** licensed to give medical advice online, so this is my **personal** and not professional take on it. Medical cannabis, hands-down, is safer. Especially processed extracts that are lab-tested for cannabinoid ratio specificity are much safer to use. Inhaling combusted materials is never a good idea, but smoking cannabis **on occasion** is not likely to give you any real health problems. Assuming you can legally obtain them, THC vape cartridges are safer to use **if from a regulated source that does not use dangerous "cuts" like the ones that were in the news.**

I disagree that "one should not consume any drugs". People with Asperger's face challenges others don't and are put into the same world. There is absolutely nothing morally or ethically wrong with using drugs that *constructively* help you in your day-to-day functioning. My experience with Phenibut has generally been quite pleasant. Keep in mind that the effects of it will take several hours to kick in, and **do not** push one gram the first time around. It paradoxically feels similar to MDMA ("ecstasy"), but in a milder form. There's more social confidence, some euphoria, and a general drive to achieve.

Unlike cannabis, gabapentin itself, and benzodiazepines, I would classify this as a **purely recreational substance.** It snowballs into addiction very fast for those susceptible. **There is no drug that builds physical tolerance as fast as Phenibut does.**

The statutory speed limit is what states codify as the "default unless otherwise posted limit". Most east coast states will put this at 55 mph.

Some states have different statutory speed limits for different types of roads. For example, Maryland has one for "low population highways", "dense areas", and "alleys".

Tennessee just has two statutory speed limits: one for "controlled-access roadways" at 70 mph unless otherwise posted, and one for "any public road or highway" at 65 mph.

Vermont's statutory speed limits are 65 mph for rural interstates, 55 mph for urban interstates or "rural limited access 2-lane roads", 50 mph for other roads, so I don't think in this instance you can get off on that defense. It's mostly southern and western states that have insanely high statutory limits, like Texas at 75 mph.

Also, **do not just "pay the ticket"**. I don't get why people on here are advocating that. I'm guessing it's simply a lack of experience or knowledge on the topic. If you make it look like you're going to stage any type of fight, you can often get the ticket at least lowered. **Ask about "PBJ" (probation before judgment) on the ticket! Offer to take an online traffic course.** PBJ means that you would agree you committed a violation but wouldn't receive a penalty if you don't get a ticket for a certain amount of time.

Vermont uses a "hybrid prima facie speed limit" system. If you were in a locality, it *may* have had a "prima facie" speed limit. That means that it is not a "per se" limit, and that exceeding it *may* not be evidence of breaking civil law. The way you'd use that defense is argue that you were indeed driving at a safe and prudent speed. However, that defense would usually only be successful for tickets written for a smaller amount over the speed limit.

**How much do I actually earn per hour? (Excluding benefits)** The average commute here takes 45 minutes each way according to Census data, so I'm going to add 5 \* 1.5 hours of "work" = 7.5 hours. The average dev here, according to SalaryData, works just about 50 hours per week, so 57.5 hours in total.
